clips.title: DORA Metrics Explained
clips.why: The industry's standard definitions of lead time and change failure rate, the two delivery numbers our job adapts.
look: Lead time measures how long a change takes from code to production; ours stops at the merge, because that is where our data ends.
Change failure rate is a share of changes that needed fixing, so it only means something next to how many changes there were.
Both are measured from events tools already record, not from asking people.
clips.after: Our nightly job computes these from fcp's GitHub history: first commit to merge, and merged PRs that a revert, hotfix or bug fix touched within 14 days.

clips.title: DORA Metrics Explained
clips.why: A short warning about using these numbers the right way, which is the reason our dashboards are team level only.
look: The metrics describe how a team's system of work behaves, not how good one person is.
Watch the trend over weeks rather than a single week's value.
clips.after: That is why no series in our job carries a login, and the delivery dashboard has a team dropdown and no person dropdown.

clips.title: The State of AI in Software Development: Data from 400+ Orgs — Justin Reock, DX
clips.why: Data on how far people's feeling of speed with AI tools is from measured speed, which is why we measure instead of asking.
look: Developers can feel faster with AI tools while the measured numbers say something else.
A survey is still useful, but next to measured numbers, not instead of them.
clips.after: Our October survey asks about time lost as well as time saved, and its answers are read next to the delivery metrics, never alone.

clips.title: The State of AI in Software Development: Data from 400+ Orgs — Justin Reock, DX
clips.why: DX's way of measuring AI in three lenses, utilization, impact and cost, which our delivery dashboard shows side by side.
look: Utilization asks whether people and agents use the tools at all.
Impact asks whether delivery changed, which needs quality next to speed.
Cost asks what it took; any one lens alone gives a misleading story.
clips.after: The job writes one series per lens and team each week, and the delivery dashboard draws the three lenses in one row over the same weeks.

practice.q: RH-1234's PR was opened as a draft at 09:00 and marked ready at 10:00. Byte, our review agent, reviewed it at 10:20 and Dana reviewed it at 14:00. What is its review wait?

options.why: Byte's review comes from a bot account. We measure how long people wait for a person, so bot reviews do not end the wait.

options.text: 4 hours, from ready to Dana's review
options.why: The clock starts when the PR asks for review, which for a draft is the moment it becomes ready, and stops at the first review by a person other than the author.

options.text: 5 hours, from opening to Dana's review
options.why: While it was a draft, nobody was asked to review it, so that hour is not waiting for review.

practice.q: Finish the filter so only a review by a person who is not the author ends the wait.
practice.hint: GitHub's GraphQL type name for a person's account, as opposed to Bot.
practice.why: GitHub marks every author as a User or a Bot. Keeping only User drops Byte and other bots; the login check drops the author's own review.

practice.q: One week the frontend team's review waits were 4, 1.5 and 48 hours. Which number should the dashboard show as the typical wait?

options.why: One PR that waited over a weekend pulls the mean far above what most PRs saw. It describes no real PR.

options.text: The median, 4 hours, with p85 and the count of 3 next to it
options.why: The median is the typical PR, p85 shows the slow tail, and the count of 3 tells the reader how little one week can say.

options.text: The maximum, 48 hours, because the worst case matters most
options.why: The worst case is useful as part of the tail, but on its own it hides that most PRs were reviewed the same day.

practice.q: Put the nightly job's work in order, from the API to the dashboard.
items: Pull last week's PRs from GitHub with their timeline events
Save the raw pull, so a fixed formula can be run again without the API
Compute one value per PR, such as its review wait
Group by team and turn the values into a median, a p85 and a count
Push the lines with the week's timestamp to VictoriaMetrics
The dashboard draws them next to the baseline line
practice.why: Raw facts first and kept, then small pure calculations, then team-level numbers with a timestamp. Each step can be checked on its own, and the baseline makes the result readable.

practice.q: The merge rate of agent PRs is a new metric: the first agent PR opened in October. What should the dashboard show for September?

options.text: 0%, because no agent PR was merged in September
options.why: A zero says agents tried and nothing merged. Drawn on a chart, it looks like a drop that never happened.

options.text: No data, because there were no agent PRs to measure
options.why: Metrics that only exist since agents started begin as no data. A missing value is honest; a zero invents a result.

options.text: The baseline value from the 12 weeks before October
options.why: The baseline is what normal looked like for metrics we already had. There is no baseline for a kind of PR that did not exist yet.
